ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ-der. Proto-Germanic *augô Proto-West Germanic *augā Old English ēage Middle English eye English eye From Middle English e, eye, eyghe, eyȝe, eȝhe, iȝe, ye, yhe, from Old English ēage, ēge (“eye”), from Proto-West Germanic *augā, from Proto-Germanic *augô (“eye”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”). Related to ogle.
Probably from rebracketing of a nye as an eye.

senses.d: An organ through which animals see (“perceive surroundings via light”).
ex: Near-synonym: eyeball
Bright lights really hurt my eyes.
The car was quite pleasing to the eye, but impractical.

senses.d: The iris of the eye, being of a specified colour.
ex: Brown, blue, green, hazel eyes.
Natalie’s brown eyes looked into Jim’s blue eyes, and the girl and boy flirted.
That dress caught her eye.

senses.d: The ability to notice what others might miss.
ex: He has an eye for talent.

senses.d: A sexually or romantically suggestive one.
ex: She was giving him the eye at the bar.

senses.d: An angry, annoyed, or malicious one.
ex: When the car cut her off, she gave him the eye.
He sought the help of an alchemist regarding remedies to ward off the eye.

senses.d: A hole at the blunt end of a needle through which thread is passed.
The oval hole of an axehead through which the axehandle is fitted.
ex: [H]e struck the Duffer a sharp blow on the back of the head with the eye of the axe, and left him stunned and senseless on the earth[.]

senses.d: To carefully or appraisingly observe (someone or something).
ex: After eyeing the document for half an hour, she decided not to sign it.
They went out and eyed the new car one last time before deciding.
Mr. Smith is eyeing a departmental reorganization plan.
Developers eyeing Merrillville as a potential spot for a data center will now have to wait a little longer to approach the Town Council.
My becomings kill me, when they do not eye well to you.

senses.d: To remove the reproductive buds from (potatoes).
ex: Once the potatoes have been rumbled they require 'eyeing' with a turning knife or hand peeler.

senses.d: To allow (fish eggs) to develop so that the black eye spots are visible.
ex: Eggs were collected from the Taylor Creek, Upper Truckee River, and Blackwood Creek traps and transported to this station to be eyed […]

senses.d: The name of the Latin script letter I/i.
ex: IED [is spoken] as "eye-ee-dee" instead of "I SPELL India Echo Delta Romeo".
an eye of pheasants

grp.label: mark on an animal resembling an eye

fr:œil.gl: eye, organ that is sensitive to light, helping organisms to see

From Early Medieval Latin traugus, a "barbarous" Latin word first attested in the Ripuarian Law, probably related to torus (“round hill”). Thought to be of Celtic, specifically Gaulish, origin. However, others have suggested a borrowing from Ancient Greek τρῦπα (trûpa, “hole”), instead.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin corūna, from Classical Latin corōna (“garland, wreath, crown”), whence also Italian corona.

ety.text: Uncertain. Possibly from Old Galician-Portuguese furaco, through Vulgar Latin *foraculum from Latin forāmen (“aperture, opening”). Compare Galician buraco, furaco, furado, Asturian furacu, buracu, Ladino burako, Leonese buraco, Spanish buraco; compare also, just for the card games, Italian burraco and Sicilian vurracu.…

Inherited from Old French convoitier, altered from the older Old French covoitier, coveitier (by analogy with the prefix con-), from Vulgar Latin *cupidietāre, a verb based on *cupidietās, a modification of the Classical Latin cupiditās by analogy with words such as medietās.
Inherited from Old French guignier, from Frankish *wingjan, from Proto-Germanic *winkaną, also the source of English wink, from Proto-Indo-European *weng- (“to bow, bend, arch, curve”).

Of Germanic origin, from Proto-Germanic *lūrni-, from the root *lūr-, *lūraną (“to spy, watch”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“to see”), similar to Dutch loens (“cross-eyed”), Latin luscus (“half-blind”).
From Vulgar Latin *adoculāre, from oclus, from Latin oculus. Compare Portuguese olhar.
From visione + -are.
